interactions.summary: Carol finishes Piccarda's answer by saying the whole kingdom wills what pleases the king and that peace consists in resting inside that will.

Jiang restates Dante's question in plain terms: if God is the center and Piccarda is in the outer sphere, does she want to move closer? A student answers that she must be content because obedience to God's will is the condition of belonging there at all.

Jiang turns the answer into a paradox: if souls are happy simply by obeying the place God assigns, heavenly hierarchy stops making sense. One student articulates the contradiction by arguing that a soul cannot both deserve the first sphere by not wanting higher happiness and still coherently advance to a better sphere.

speaker_notes.note: The student's line is elliptical and appears to refer back to Jiang's earlier insistence that God is not simply assigning people to slots as a judge. The usable point is that the hierarchy starts to look judicial once placement is treated as God's decision.

claims.claim: Piccarda's speech concludes that the whole kingdom wills what pleases the king and that peace is found within that will.
Jiang reframes Dante's question as whether a soul in the outer sphere wants to move inward and get closer to God.
A student argues that Piccarda is content because absolute obedience to God requires contentment with the sphere God assigned her.

Jiang argues that if heavenly happiness is just obedience to God's placement, the hierarchy of spheres becomes logically incoherent because no soul could meaningfully want or deserve a higher station.

A student sharpens the paradox by arguing that if desiring a higher sphere disqualifies you from the lower one, and forced advancement would make you less happy, then the hierarchy cannot function consistently.

signature_moments.moment: Piccarda's peace is defined as willing exactly what the king wills.
signature_moments.source_phrase: in his will there is our peace
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the packet its cleanest formulation of paradise as desire synchronized with divine rule rather than as private fulfillment.

signature_moments.moment: The student exposes the hierarchy trap: wanting a higher sphere disqualifies you, but not wanting it makes promotion unintelligible.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if you want to advance to the second sphere that you are not even worthy of the first sphere
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the most precise statement of the contradiction Jiang wants the class to feel inside Dante's paradise.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang states the paradox in blunt classroom terms: if everyone simply obeys, there should be no hierarchy in heaven at all.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if it was just a case where you just obey God's will and then everyone's in heaven there'll be no hierarchy in heaven
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns a theological subtlety into a structural problem about why paradise has ranks in the first place.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The ranked structure of paradise that Jiang says becomes paradoxical if every soul is already perfectly content with its assigned place.
Jiang's classroom shorthand for Piccarda's distance from the divine center, used to restate Dante's question about whether she wants to move closer to God.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture shifts from naming the lowest sphere's inhabitants to pressing on the internal logic of paradise itself. Jiang no longer treats Piccarda's peace as the end of the matter; he turns it into a contradiction between contentment, hierarchy, and advancement.

uncertainty_notes.note: Segment 0389 is terse and partly dependent on prior discussion. Preserve only the stable point that the student hears a judging placement logic emerging, rather than over-specifying the objection.
